claims.text: Formation and persistence of a stable protective oxide on CrFeCoNiX above 900 °C is governed by the alloy's microstructural phase homogeneity.
Single-phase CrFeCoNiX alloys have uniformly distributed cations, particularly Cr and X.
Uniform distribution of Cr and X in a single-phase CrFeCoNiX alloy promotes formation of an entropy-stabilized oxide.
Configurational entropy can stabilize a homogeneous, single-phase multication oxide.
The entropy-stabilized surface oxide on CrFeCoNiX is continuous and coherent.
An entropy-stabilized oxide scale minimizes oxide–alloy interfacial stress.
Multiphase CrFeCoNiX alloys contain compositionally segregated regions.
Compositional segregation in multiphase CrFeCoNiX produces spatially heterogeneous oxide formation and differential oxidation rates.
Differences in thermal properties between segregated regions create local stress concentrations in the oxide scale.
Local stresses arising from differential thermal expansion cause oxide-scale cracking and spallation.
A continuous oxide on a single-phase CrFeCoNiX alloy accommodates thermal expansion better and develops lower internal stress than the oxide on a multiphase alloy.
Above 900 °C in oxidative or mildly corrosive atmospheres, single-phase CrFeCoNiX alloys will maintain a stable, adherent oxide with minimal spallation.
Under identical exposure, multiphase CrFeCoNiX alloys will form unstable oxide scales that crack and spall.
The proposed behavior applies to CrFeCoNiX alloys for X equal to Si, Mn, or Al.
The proposed behavior is bounded to temperatures above 900 °C and oxidative or mildly corrosive atmospheres.
The relative influence of Si, Mn, and Al on oxide-scale formation and stability is not fully defined.
The quantitative contribution of entropy stabilization relative to oxidation kinetics is uncertain.
